method: For each corner it takes the best low-cost fix the evidence supports without a site visit (brief.SUPPORTED: measured in this city, the record FHWA cites, or the median of national studies whose conditions the record shows), and keeps apart the larger "textbook" estimate that would need a site check or that the city's own record contradicts. One fix per corner, never added together at a corner (the Highway Safety Manual's simple method does not allow stacking).
caveats: Estimates use the Highway Safety Manual's simple method; a qualified engineer must review each fix.
One fix per corner; totals add corners, so a crash near two corners can count twice.
The regression-to-the-mean factor is measured within the listed corners, so it is a lower bound on that effect where the corners were themselves picked by the same records.

letter.to: the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA)
letter.subject: 50 high-crash intersections on your roads
letter.body: In the 5 years of public police crash records up to 2026-10-31, the 50 high-crash intersections in San Francisco where we take you to be responsible for at least one of the roads, because the state's road inventory does not list them had 768 injury crashes that the records place at them (a crash placed at two of them counts for each). At 40 of them, a low-cost fix the evidence supports would avoid about 20.8 crashes a year, worth about $7.0 million a year at the U.S. DOT's values. At 7 more, a fix needs a site check first; the table names what to check. The table lists each intersection, the fix and the evidence behind it. We ask for a safety review at each intersection and for the fixes listed, and a reply on which you will take up.
